title: Turning the Signal Off: Arrestins, RGS Proteins and Phosphodiesterases

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: A response that fades while the stimulus continues is {{c1::desensitization}}.
cards.quote: A response that fades while the stimulus continues is desensitization.

cards.front: In a GPCR response, when does each active layer (receptor, G protein, messenger, phosphorylated target) fade?
cards.back: When removal outruns production. At each layer, the question is whether active material is made faster or removed faster.
cards.quote: During a GPCR response, each active layer fades when removal outruns production.

cards.front: List the six removal steps that can end a GPCR response, from the outside in.
cards.back: The ligand leaves; the receptor loses access to its G protein; the receptor is taken inside in a vesicle; G-alpha hydrolyzes its GTP; a phosphodiesterase destroys cyclic AMP; phosphatases reset the targets.
cards.why: A pathway need not use every one.
cards.quote: the ligand leaves; the receptor loses access to its G protein; the receptor is taken inside in a vesicle; G-alpha hydrolyzes its GTP;

cards.front: Arrestin uncoupling or loss of IP3 receptors makes a response fade even though the stimulus is unchanged. How does this work?
cards.back: It cuts the active material made per unit of stimulus, so removal wins at the same stimulus. This is desensitization from the production side.
cards.quote: Desensitization works from the production side: arrestin uncoupling or a loss of IP3 receptors cuts the active material made per unit of stimulus

cards.front: What does a G-protein-coupled receptor kinase (GRK) do, and to which receptors?
cards.back: It writes the phosphate mark, and it preferentially marks the active receptor.
cards.quote: The writer, a G-protein-coupled receptor kinase (GRK), preferentially marks the active receptor.
cards.section: The experiment: the mark is necessary but not sufficient

cards.front: Which experiment showed that the kinase marking the beta-adrenergic receptor is not protein kinase A and that it recognizes the active receptor?
cards.back: An extract of kin⁻ S49 cells (no working protein kinase A) still phosphorylated receptor in vesicles with radioactive ATP. Isoproterenol increased it and alprenolol blocked the increase.
cards.why: A genetic control avoids trusting an inhibitor's completeness and specificity.
cards.quote: Isoproterenol increased that phosphorylation, whereas alprenolol blocked the increase, showing that the kinase recognized the active receptor.
cards.section: The experiment: the mark is necessary but not sufficient

cards.front: Why is the protein that reads the receptor's phosphate mark called arrestin?
cards.back: It was first found in retina, working with rhodopsin kinase, and it arrested rhodopsin's function.
cards.quote: It was later named arrestin because it arrested rhodopsin's function.
cards.section: The experiment: the mark is necessary but not sufficient

cards.front: How much did the non-retinal beta-arrestin reduce signaling by the kinase-marked beta-adrenergic receptor, and did it act on rhodopsin?
cards.back: By more than 75%. It did not act on rhodopsin.
cards.quote: It reduced signaling by the kinase-marked receptor by more than 75% and did not act on rhodopsin.
cards.section: The experiment: the mark is necessary but not sufficient

cards.front: In the reconstitution, purified kinase alone put about 8 phosphates on each beta-adrenergic receptor. What did that show about the mark?
cards.back: The receptors could still switch on Gs, so the phosphate mark is necessary but not sufficient to silence the receptor.
cards.quote: With the pure kinase alone, the receptors carried an average of about 8 phosphates each and could still switch on Gs.

cards.front: A kinase batch purified 350-fold cut G-protein activation by up to 80%. The 20,000-fold pure kinase still phosphorylated receptors but cut it by only 10 to 15%. What would you add back to test your explanation, and what result is expected?
cards.back: Add back the lost second protein, arrestin. Kinase plus arrestin cut activity to about 59% of untreated receptor, a loss of about 40%.
cards.why: Phosphorylation still happened, so a second component needed for switch-off was lost on purification.
cards.quote: With kinase and arrestin together, activity fell to about 59% of the untreated receptor's, a loss of about 40%.

cards.front: Arrestin is added to beta-adrenergic receptor that the kinase never marked. What happens to Gs activation, and what does this show?
cards.back: Almost nothing: activity stayed at 98.1% of the value without arrestin (13 measurements). Arrestin needs the mark to block the G protein.
cards.quote: Arrestin added to a receptor the kinase had never marked left activity at 98.1% of the value without arrestin, across 13 measurements.

cards.front: Why did the reconstitution test bovine serum albumin and heat-denatured arrestin in place of arrestin?
cards.back: They are controls for a nonspecific protein effect. Neither could substitute, so the loss of activity needs active arrestin.
cards.quote: Neither bovine serum albumin, an unrelated protein, nor heat-denatured arrestin could substitute for arrestin.

cards.front: Which coat protein do beta-arrestin 1 and 2 bind directly, and what does this let arrestin do beyond blocking the G protein?
cards.back: Clathrin. Arrestin can pull the receptor into a coated pit, carrying it into the cell.
cards.quote: beta-arrestin 1 and beta-arrestin 2 bind clathrin directly and tightly.
cards.section: Arrestin carries the receptor into the cell

cards.front: A hybrid arrestin binds the marked receptor but cannot bind clathrin. Predict what happens to G-protein coupling and to receptor uptake.
cards.back: It should still uncouple the receptor if it covers the core, but carry the receptor in less well. Uptake needs both contacts.
cards.quote: uptake needs both contacts: the protein that blocks the G protein's site also pulls the receptor into a coated pit.
cards.section: Arrestin carries the receptor into the cell

cards.front: Once arrestin replaces the G protein on a receptor, which partners can it bind besides clathrin?
cards.back: The adaptor AP-2, Src, and parts of the ERK and JNK kinase cascades. How much signaling this supports without a G protein is debated.
cards.quote: besides clathrin and the adaptor AP-2, it can bind Src and parts of the ERK and JNK kinase cascades.
cards.section: Arrestin carries the receptor into the cell

cards.front: An agonist-occupied receptor has been taken into an early endosome. Is it necessarily out of service?
cards.back: No. Active receptor and G protein were found at the early endosome membrane, so location does not tell you whether a receptor is still signaling.
cards.why: Rule: an occupied receptor loses its G protein only when a dedicated protein acts on it.
cards.quote: an occupied receptor loses its G protein only when a dedicated protein acts on it, and where it sits does not tell you whether it is still signaling.
cards.section: Arrestin carries the receptor into the cell

cards.front: Which two findings would break the rule that an occupied receptor loses its G protein only when a dedicated protein acts on it?
cards.back: An occupied receptor that uncouples with nothing acting on it (no mark, reader or other bound protein), or a receptor that stops signaling every time it leaves the surface, in every cell tested.
cards.quote: Two findings would break the rule: an occupied receptor that uncouples with nothing acting on it
cards.section: Arrestin carries the receptor into the cell

cards.front: What did RGS4 and GAIP do to Gi alpha-1 in vitro?
cards.back: They accelerated its GTP hydrolysis at least 40-fold, and they acted on the other Gi-family subunits tested.
cards.quote: RGS4 and GAIP accelerated GTP hydrolysis by Gi alpha-1 at least 40-fold and acted on the other Gi-family subunits tested.

cards.front: RGS4 is added to active, GTP-bound Gs alpha, the subunit in the beta-adrenergic example. Predict the effect on its GTP-bound lifetime.
cards.back: Little or none. RGS4 and GAIP did not act on Gs, so the name of the family does not guarantee action on every G-alpha subunit.
cards.quote: They did not act on Gs, the alpha subunit in the beta-adrenergic example.

cards.front: A phosphodiesterase turns cyclic AMP into {{c1::AMP}}, which does not activate protein kinase A.
cards.quote: A phosphodiesterase turns cyclic AMP into AMP, which does not activate protein kinase A.

cards.front: With constant synthesis and first-order breakdown, messenger level at steady state = {{c1::rate of synthesis ÷ rate constant of breakdown}}.
cards.quote: messenger level at steady state = rate of synthesis ÷ rate constant of breakdown

cards.front: A cell makes a messenger at a constant 3 µM per second and removes it by first-order breakdown with rate constant 6 per second. A drug cuts the enzyme's activity by half, and synthesis is unchanged. What are the steady levels before and after?
cards.back: Before: 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5 µM. After: the rate constant is 3 per second, so 3 ÷ 3 = 1 µM, a twofold rise.
cards.why: At steady state synthesis equals breakdown.
cards.quote: At steady state synthesis equals breakdown, so: messenger level at steady state = rate of synthesis ÷ rate constant of breakdown

cards.front: Caffeine inhibits phosphodiesterases in a test tube. Why is this not the best account of a few cups of coffee?
cards.back: At the concentrations a few cups produce, most of its effect is thought to come from blocking adenosine receptors.
cards.quote: at the concentrations a few cups produce, most of its effect is thought to come from blocking adenosine receptors.

cards.front: Which enzyme does sildenafil inhibit, and which messenger does that protect?
cards.back: Phosphodiesterase 5, which breaks down cyclic GMP.
cards.quote: Sildenafil, the cleaner example, inhibits phosphodiesterase 5, which breaks down cyclic GMP, a close relative of cyclic AMP.

cards.front: Sildenafil reaches blood-vessel smooth muscle. Compare cyclic GMP and relaxation where nitric oxide is present with where it is absent.
cards.back: With nitric oxide, cyclic GMP is made and the muscle relaxes; sildenafil makes that signal larger and longer. Without it, no cyclic GMP is made, so the level stays low and there is no added relaxation.
cards.why: Slowing breakdown cannot raise a level that has no synthesis behind it.
cards.quote: Nitric oxide starts cyclic GMP synthesis in the smooth muscle of some blood vessels, and the muscle relaxes; sildenafil makes that existing signal larger and longer.

cards.front: Which enzyme class removes the phosphate that protein kinase A added to a target?
cards.back: A protein phosphatase, the last removal layer.
cards.quote: At the last layer, a protein phosphatase removes the phosphate protein kinase A added

cards.front: How is the RGS protein GAIP held on a membrane?
cards.back: By palmitate, a fatty acid bonded to the protein.
cards.quote: GAIP is held on a membrane by palmitate, a fatty acid bonded to the protein.

cards.front: In rhesus monkeys with hypothalamic lesions that abolished gonadotropin release, how did hourly GnRH compare with constant GnRH infusion?
cards.back: Hourly GnRH restored sustained gonadotropin secretion. A constant infusion did not, so pulses preserve a response that steady stimulation shuts down.
cards.quote: GnRH given once an hour restored sustained secretion; a constant infusion did not.
cards.section: Constant GnRH shuts the pituitary down

cards.front: Why can a GRK mark plus arrestin not be the whole explanation for GnRH receptor desensitization?
cards.back: The mammalian type I GnRH receptor lacks a C-terminal tail, resists agonist-dependent phosphorylation, and resists rapid desensitization.
cards.quote: The mammalian type I GnRH receptor lacks a C-terminal tail, resists agonist-dependent phosphorylation, and resists rapid desensitization.
cards.section: Constant GnRH shuts the pituitary down

cards.front: A suitable C-terminal tail with phosphorylation sites is added to the GnRH receptor. Predict the effect on rapid agonist-dependent desensitization, and say what this does not show.
cards.back: Rapid desensitization should increase. It does not show that the missing tail explains long-term pituitary shutdown.
cards.quote: Tail-addition experiments support this, tying the missing tail to resistance against the rapid route, but they do not show that the tail explains long-term pituitary shutdown.
cards.section: Constant GnRH shuts the pituitary down

cards.front: Cells stop responding after a day of constant agonist. Which three measurements locate the block?
cards.back: Count surface receptors, measure second messenger made per dose, and bypass the receptor with another stimulus.
cards.quote: To locate the longer-term block, count surface receptors, measure second messenger made per dose, and bypass the receptor.
cards.section: Constant GnRH shuts the pituitary down

cards.front: In a bypass test on desensitized cells, what does rescue by the bypass stimulus imply, and what does continued failure imply?
cards.back: Rescue implicates a bypassed step. Continued failure puts the block farther downstream, below where the bypass enters.
cards.quote: rescue implicates a bypassed step, and continued failure puts the block farther downstream.
cards.section: Constant GnRH shuts the pituitary down

cards.front: After a day of constant agonist, hypothetical pituitary cells release 10% of their starting gonadotropin. Surface receptors are 40% of start, messenger made per dose is 35%, and a calcium ionophore restores release to 95%. Where is the main block?
cards.back: At the receptor level. Receptor number and messenger output both fell, and a bypass that enters below the receptor rescues release.
cards.why: Compare with data where receptors and messenger stay near normal and the bypass also fails: block downstream.
cards.quote: A receptor-level failure lowers receptor number or messenger output; a downstream failure can leave both relatively intact while secretion falls.
cards.section: Constant GnRH shuts the pituitary down

cards.front: In gonadotrope cell lines, what is the best-studied change under sustained GnRH that makes the calcium response fade?
cards.back: A fast loss of the IP3 receptors that release calcium. How much this explains in a patient on a GnRH agonist is less settled.
cards.quote: sustained GnRH causes a fast loss of the IP3 receptors that release calcium, so the calcium response fades.
cards.section: Constant GnRH shuts the pituitary down

cards.front: How does what a GRK reads differ from what protein kinases A and C read, and how does their reach differ?
cards.back: A GRK reads receptor shape and marks mainly agonist-occupied receptors, silencing those being hit (homologous). Kinases A and C read messengers, so they act cell-wide (heterologous).
cards.quote: A GRK reads receptor shape, so it marks mainly agonist-occupied receptors.

cards.front: A cell has high cyclic AMP from hormone A, and receptors for hormone B carry protein kinase A target sites. Predict the response to hormone B, and contrast it with a receptor silenced by GRK and arrestin.
cards.back: Hormone B's receptors can be phosphorylated and weakened even when empty (heterologous). GRK and arrestin silence mainly the receptors being hit, so the cell can still answer a different hormone.
cards.why: Rule: messenger-reading kinases act cell-wide when messenger is high.
cards.quote: Kinases A and C read messengers, so they can mark any receptor carrying their sites, occupied or empty, including receptors for a different hormone.

cards.front: A cell is held in constant agonist and given a phosphodiesterase inhibitor. Receptor uncoupling by arrestin still occurs. Will the cyclic AMP response still fade, and will the inhibitor change its level?
cards.back: It should still fade, because uncoupling cuts the cyclic AMP made per unit of stimulus. The inhibitor lowers the breakdown constant, so the level is higher, but cannot stop the fall in synthesis.
cards.why: Rests on level = synthesis ÷ breakdown constant, and on production-side desensitization.
cards.quote: At each layer, ask whether active material is being made faster or removed faster.
